name: Diego Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I'm a carpenter for a big house builder on a new estate, two hundred homes, doing first fix: floor joists, stud walls, stair openings. I'm on site at seven and we work to a tight programme, house after house. Then evenings and Saturdays I run my own little business, Costa Garden Rooms, building decks and garden offices. I rent a garage unit for the tools and the timber.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you run the side business?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly from my phone with AI. It drafts my quotes, turns a customer's rough sketch into a 3D design they can spin around, writes my posts for local social media, and helps me order the right amount of timber so I don't waste money. I check everything, but it saves me about ten hours a week. Ana, my girlfriend, says I talk to the chatbot more than to her, which is a bit true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'll keep using what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great tool if you use it right and it's not the end of the world. I'd probably post a little video showing how I use it to quote a deck in ten minutes. Good for business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's ideal, honestly. I've got the tools, the garage, about a year of savings, and a growing side business. A plateau means I keep using AI to get ahead of the guys who don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both jobs going this year and push the garden rooms harder, maybe aim for twenty builds instead of twelve. If it kept growing I'd go full-time on my own business in about eighteen months. I'd put money into a second van and a better saw bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually quite fired up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's holding you back from going full-time now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The steady pay from the house builder, and my dad's voice in my head saying don't give up a sure thing. He ran a small café for twenty years and it nearly broke him twice. I want to be sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe the guys on site who think a phone is just for calls. They'll miss out, but that's their choice.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a great tool if you use it right and not the end of the world. I'd post a video showing how I quote a deck in ten minutes, which is good for business.
S0.think: It's ideal for him: tools, a garage unit, about a year of savings and a growing side business. A plateau means he keeps using AI to stay ahead of those who don't.
S0.do: Keeps both jobs going and aims for twenty garden-room builds instead of twelve, going full-time on his own in about eighteen months if it grows. Invests in a second van and a better saw bench.
S0.quote: He ran a small café for twenty years and it nearly broke him twice.
S0.fieldNote: Diego is an enterprising carpenter who already treats AI as a business tool. His caution about going full-time comes from his father's hard years with a café. He sees non-users as making their own choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's opportunity. That's how I'd see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and people who move with it will do well. I'd say the government shouldn't get in the way too much, let businesses figure it out, and help people with apprenticeships and training rather than handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the house builder job might shrink, because those estates are repetitive and factories can make a lot of it. But my garden rooms are custom, and I'm faster than anyone around with the design side. I'd come out ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time on Costa Garden Rooms within a year, and hire one other carpenter. I'd buy a small CNC cutter, around eight thousand, so I can pre-cut garden room kits in the garage. And I'd use AI for everything in the office: quotes, scheduling, invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, mainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hire someone. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Tomás, who's just finished his trade certificate. Family first. I'd teach him the AI side too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana think of you leaving the steady job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be nervous but she'd back me. She's got a steady job as a dental hygienist, so we'd have one sure income. And we'd pray about it, like we do with all the big stuff.

S1.say: I'd say people who move with the change will do well, and government shouldn't get in the way too much. It should help with apprenticeships and training rather than handouts.
S1.think: His house builder job might shrink because estates are repetitive, but custom garden rooms and his speed with design would put him ahead.
S1.do: Goes full-time on his garden-room business within a year and hires his cousin. Buys a small CNC cutter for about eight thousand to pre-cut kits, and uses AI for quotes, scheduling and invoices.
S1.quote: And we'd pray about it, like we do with all the big stuff.
S1.fieldNote: Diego sees disruption as his moment to go independent. His values show in hiring family and praying over decisions. He favours markets, training and apprenticeships over state support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots doing everything. Okay. That changes the game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses that adapt fast will survive and people should get moving instead of complaining. Government should keep things open so small businesses can buy the robots too, not just the big companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit worried. If an AI can design and a robot can build a garden room, my edge is gone, unless I own the robots. And if loads of people lose their jobs, who's going to buy a garden office?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the house builder job as long as it lasted, for the steady pay. I'd put a big chunk of savings into whatever building robots I could get early and try to be the local guy who owns them. I'd keep some cash back, because if customers dry up, I need to survive a slow year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited and worried at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying robots early a big gamble with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is. But sitting still is a gamble too. I'd rather bet on owning something than on being needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speed. In two years, the big companies get the robots first and small guys like me get squeezed. With more time, robots get cheaper and I can buy in.

S2.say: I'd say businesses that adapt fast will survive and people should get moving instead of complaining. Government should keep markets open so small businesses can buy robots too, not just big companies.
S2.think: He'd be somewhat worried, because AI design and robot building would erase his edge unless he owned the robots. And if many people lose jobs, he wonders who will still buy garden offices.
S2.do: Keeps the house builder job while it lasts, puts a big chunk of savings into early building robots to become the local owner of them, and holds back cash to survive a slow year.
S2.feel: Uneasy, excited and worried at once.
S2.quote: I'd rather bet on owning something than on being needed.
S2.fieldNote: Diego's answer to AGI is ownership, not resistance or retraining. He's aware his customers' incomes would collapse too, which worries him more than the machines. He's willing to gamble savings because standing still also feels risky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a better runway for a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for anyone willing to work, so get learning and get building. I'd say small businesses need fair access to the new robots and less red tape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is just about right for me. I'd build up the garden rooms business, learn the robots as they come in, and by 2031 I'd have a proper company that owns its machines. I'd be thirty-two and, if it goes right, a boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go full-time on my business, hire Tomás and buy the CNC cutter. Over the next few years I'd add robots as prices drop and maybe open a small showroom. I'd keep a year of costs in the bank for safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a good plan coming together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the house builder lads?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some will come work for me, I hope. Others will need to retrain. I'd like to offer apprenticeships, because that's how I learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if customers can't afford garden rooms when jobs go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the real risk, I know. I'd probably switch to repairs and practical things people still need, like extensions for families moving in together. I'd follow the work.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time for anyone willing to work, so get learning and building. Small businesses need fair access to new robots and less red tape.
S3.think: Five years is about right for him to build the business and learn robots as they arrive, so by 2031 he'd own a proper company with its own machines. At 32, if it went right, he'd be a boss.
S3.do: Goes full-time on his business, hires his cousin and buys the CNC cutter in the first year. Adds robots as prices fall, maybe opens a small showroom and keeps a year of costs in the bank.
S3.feel: Calm, like a good plan coming together.
S3.quote: I'd probably switch to repairs and practical things people still need, like extensions for families moving in together.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Diego sees a clear path to running a company that owns its machines. He gives a practical answer to the risk that customers lose income. He'd offer apprenticeships to former colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's loads of time to build something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a huge chance for people who get ready, so get your skills and your business sorted. Government should back apprenticeships and small firms, not pay people to sit around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well. Ten years to grow a company, buy machines when they're cheap and maybe own a couple of properties. I'd be thirty-seven, married with kids I hope, and running my own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time on the business next year, grow it steadily, and add AI and robots step by step as they prove themselves. I'd invest some profits in a rental property. I'd train Tomás and a couple of apprentices along the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the end point bother you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If robots can do everything, I'd hope people still want someone they trust running the job. I'm counting on that, and I know it's a bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Own something, work hard, and look after your family. Don't wait for anyone to hand you a life. That's what my dad told me, and he was right, even if the café nearly killed him.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a huge chance for people who get ready, so get your skills and business sorted. Government should back apprenticeships and small firms, not pay people to sit around.
S4.think: He thinks he'd do well, with ten years to grow a company, buy machines cheaply and maybe own a couple of properties. At 37 he hopes to be married with children and running his own business.
S4.do: Goes full-time on the business next year, grows it steadily and adds AI and robots as they prove themselves. Invests profits in a rental property and trains his cousin and apprentices.
S4.quote: Don't wait for anyone to hand you a life.
S4.fieldNote: Diego is openly optimistic about the long timeline and sees ten years as a runway to ownership. He admits his business bet rests on people still wanting a trusted person in charge. Family, faith and self-reliance tie his answers together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the big companies would get the robots first and small businesses like mine would get squeezed. What would help is fair access to the machines for small firms, less red tape, and apprenticeships so young people can still get a start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like to build something for a customer who becomes a friend. I built a garden office for a widow last spring, and she still sends me a card at Christmas. A robot doesn't get the card.

headlineQuote: A robot doesn't get the card.
portrait: Diego Costa is a 27-year-old first-fix carpenter on a big housing estate who runs his own garden-room business on evenings and weekends, using AI every day for quotes, designs and marketing. He has about a year of savings, his own tools and a rented garage unit, and lives with his girlfriend Ana, a dental hygienist. Faith, family and self-reliance shape his views, and he sees change as a chance to own his own firm. Only the two-year AGI picture makes him uneasy, because big companies would get the robots first; with more time he plans to go independent and own the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because big companies would get the robots first and small businesses like his would be squeezed.
whatWouldHelp: Fair access to the machines for small firms, less red tape, and apprenticeships so young people can still get started.
